readerTitle: Your biggest supplier just raised prices 12%. Four moves to answer it.
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (선반 제조사와 철강 공급사) + 가상 적용 (소프트웨어 회사와 지도 API 공급사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 큰 공급사와의 재협상은 '가격을 깎는 싸움'이 아니라, 대안을 먼저 확보하고, 상대의 압박을 이해하고, 여러 조건을 맞바꾸고, 조건부로만 양보하는 순서의 문제다.
misconception: 가장 큰 공급사에는 협상력이 없으니 인상을 받아들이거나, 반대로 강하게 위협해야만 가격을 지킬 수 있다.

sources.text: 협상론의 표준 개념 (BATNA, 조건부 양보, 다중 이슈 교환, 감정 라벨링)
모든 수치와 회사는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 공급사의 여름 유휴 설비, 급주문 비용 등은 시나리오 설정입니다. 실제 철강 산업 통계로 읽히지 않도록 카드에 illustrative 표시를 유지하세요.
소프트웨어 사례의 40% 인상, 2년 약정 등은 가상 설정이며 특정 API 업체를 가리키지 않습니다.

cards.title: The letter arrives on a Monday.
body: You run a company that makes steel shelving for warehouses. One steel mill supplies most of your metal, about **$2 million** a year.
Their letter is short: prices rise 12% in 60 days. That's $240,000 a year, more than your whole profit last year.
You have four decisions to make. Pick each one before you read on.

image.label: A supplier letter on a workbench beside steel coils
image.brief: 공장 작업대 위에 놓인 한 장짜리 편지. 큰 글씨로 "+12%"가 보이고, 뒤로 철강 코일과 반쯤 조립된 창고 선반. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음. 약간 긴장감 있는 아침 조명.

cards.title: What do you do first?
body: The mill is bigger than you, and switching would take months. Your production manager wants to call them today.

options.text: Call today and push back hard before the date gets close
options.feedback: You'd negotiate with nothing behind your words. If they say no, your only move left is to accept.

options.text: Quietly get a quote from another mill first, and work out your limit
options.feedback: A second mill quotes 9% above today's price, after three months of testing. Now you know your floor: anything below +9% beats walking away.

options.text: Accept the rise to protect a key relationship
options.feedback: The relationship stays calm, but you pay $240,000 a year without ever learning whether you had to.

cards.title: Say you chose B. Now, the first meeting.
body: The mill's sales manager opens: "Energy and labor costs went up. We have no choice." How do you respond?

options.feedback: The threat makes them defend the number. They hold at 12% and the meeting ends cold.

options.text: "It sounds like your costs have squeezed you hard, and you're under pressure to pass them on."
options.feedback: Naming their pressure lowers their guard. She admits what hurts most: idle machines in summer and costly rush orders from customers like you.

options.text: "Could we meet in the middle at 6%?"
options.feedback: You might get 6%, but you gave away half your ground before learning anything about what they need.

cards.title: Say you chose B. What goes on the table?
body: You now know two things the mill cares about besides price: steady summer volume and fewer rush orders.

options.text: Stick to price only and ask for no increase at all
options.feedback: With one issue, every gain for you is a loss for them. You reach a deadlock in a week.

options.text: Offer a firm 12-month forecast and shift orders into summer, in return for a smaller rise
options.feedback: Planning ahead costs you little and is worth a lot to them. They come back at 8%.

options.text: Offer to pay invoices in 10 days instead of 45
options.feedback: They'd like it, but fast payment ties up your own cash. It's a real cost, not a cheap trade.

cards.title: Say you chose B. They offer 8%. You hoped for 4%.
body: Your limit is 9%. Their offer is good, but you think there's more room. How do you move?

options.text: Jump to 6% to show good faith
options.feedback: A big, free step tells them you have plenty more to give. They wait for the next one.

options.text: Move to 5%, but only if the price holds for 12 months
options.feedback: A small step with a condition attached. They accept 5% with a 12-month price hold.

options.text: Say 4% is final and go quiet
options.feedback: It might work, but a hard line with no reason invites a stalemate you can't afford in 60 days.

cards.title: The same supplier, three different prices.
body: Your forecast and summer orders cost you some planning effort. In return you pay **$140,000 less** a year than the letter demanded, with the price locked for a year.
cards.softwareNote: The same four moves work when your biggest supplier is a cloud host or a data API. Usage forecasts and longer commitments are the summer orders of software.

cards.title: These moves have limits.
body: Your backup quote must be real. Bluffing about an alternative can wreck trust with a supplier you'll deal with for years.
The supplier needs a margin too. Squeeze too hard and you may become the customer they serve last when supply gets tight.
And sometimes the rise is fair. If their costs truly jumped and your backup costs more, a fast, friendly yes can be the right call.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your delivery-tracking app relies on a mapping data provider. At renewal, they announce a 40% price rise. Your code depends on their service, and switching would take months.

options.text: Tell them you're switching next month unless they drop it
options.feedback: They likely know how deep their service sits in your code. A threat you can't carry out weakens you.

options.text: Start testing an alternative, ask what's driving the rise, then offer a two-year commitment and usage forecast for a smaller increase
options.feedback: You build a real alternative, learn their pressure, and trade something they value. It's the same path as the steel mill.

options.text: Accept and pass the full cost on to your users
options.feedback: Quick and calm, but you may push users to cheaper rivals over a cost you never tested.

cards.title: Prepare, listen, trade, then concede on conditions.
body: Each decision used one idea from this unit:
**Try it today:** pick your biggest supplier. Write down your walk-away option and two things besides price that they would value.
list: **Get a backup quote first:** negotiating from a weak position
**Add forecasts and timing:** many issues at once
